title: The Medina charter
hookLine: a written charter binds Muslims, Jews and others of the city in mutual defense

cards: No police, no courts, no city council. Just families and clans, each with its own old grudges, and one newcomer they have agreed to listen to.
Different languages in the lanes, different holidays, different loyalties, the same streets. That was Medina. Arab clans, some of them Muslim now and some not.
Jewish tribes who had lived there for generations. Newcomers from Mecca, with nothing. What do you do with a city like that?
According to the early biographers, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had it written down.

teach.b: It's often called the Constitution of Medina, or the Medina charter. Its text reaches us through the early biographer Ibn Ishaq, and through another early scholar, Abu 'Ubayd. It's a list of agreements.
Each clan pays its own blood money and ransoms its own captives, as before. Nobody shelters a murderer.
If the city is attacked, everyone defends it together and shares the cost. Disputes go to God and to Muhammad. Then the lines people still quote.
The believers, from Mecca and from Medina, and those who join them and strive with them, are one ummah, one community, distinct from other people.

And the Jews of one clan, the charter says, are an ummah alongside the believers: to the Jews their religion, and to the Muslims theirs. The word ummah shares a root with umm, mother, and imam, the one in front.

teach.h: UMMAH — A PEOPLE AROUND A CENTER.
teach.b: An ummah is a people gathered around a center. Here it works in more than one way at once: the community of believers, and a wider civic community of the city, bound by promises. Historians such as R.
B. Serjeant treat the text as early, and Serjeant argued it joins several agreements made at different times.
Honesty matters here too: relations with some of Medina's Jewish tribes later broke down, and the path will come to that.
But today is the beginning: one written page that tried to make one city out of many peoples.

how: Muslims today use ummah above all for the worldwide community of believers, and some point to the Medina charter when they talk about how Muslims can live with neighbors of other faiths under shared promises.

games.q: you're in charge of a city of rival clans and several faiths, with no courts. what do you do first?
o: let each clan settle its own feuds.
games.why: the charter wrote down the promises: defend the city together, shelter no murderer, and to each their religion.

practice: Picture the people who live closest to you: next door, across the hall, above, below.
For each one, notice honestly whether you know their name, with no guilt, then picture the one you'd most like to know and the moment you might ask: at the mailbox, in the elevator, over the fence.
If you pray, you can make du'a for them.

wordCard.voice: Ummah. A community, a people gathered around a center: in the charter, both the believers and the whole city bound by promises. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a community, a people. the same root gives umm, mother, and imam, the one in front.

carryVoice: Your line: one city, many peoples. Old customs kept, new promises written down. That's day two hundred sixty.
